Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Although the single-brain approach has considerably advanced our knowledge of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying social cognition, a major limitation is that participants are not actively involved in real-time social interactions (Czeszumski et al., 2022; Schilbach & Redcay, 2025).

> To confirm this latter criterion, participants were screened using the short version of the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID IV; Wittchen et al., 1997).

> Participants were then interviewed by a psychologist, if necessary, to verify their suitability for the study.

> Participants were recruited through flyers in university buildings and social media platforms.

> After voluntary written informed consent was obtained, participants received verbal instructions about the study and task instructions using pre-recorded videos to ensure consistency of instructions across pairs.

> Participants were not allowed to communicate during the task instructions in order to prevent any prior coordination.

> Following the scanner session, participants completed self-report questionnaires using the "Sosci survey" online platform (https://www.soscisurvey.de/).

> Participants completed all blocks in the same order, as preregistered.

> It is possible that during easy blocks, participants were similarly thinking about their partner's intentions and actions.

> Two participants are simultaneously scanned, and task activity is synchronized through a server.

Ethics approval statement:

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Exploring the intra- and inter-brain underpinnings of cooperative, dominant, and aggressive behavior in sibling relationships.
table.research_questions:
Overall aim: to investigate the neural underpinnings of intra- and inter- brain activity during sibling interactions, specifically during cooperative, competitive, dominant, and aggressive behavior. 

Cooperative task (CoTT):
1.	Validation: We expect that pairs with higher INS will perform better (described as deleting more lines) in the CoTT task. Moreover, we expect that participants will have higher INS during easy compared to complex trials. 
2.	Group comparison: We expect cooperative pairs to perform better and have higher INS than competitive pairs. 
3.	Leadership: We expect that leader-follower pairs will perform better and have higher INS than follower-follower pairs. 
*Leader participant is defined as the participant who makes the first moves more frequently (indicating the direction he/she wants to take). 
4.	Feedback: We expect that positive feedback will increase INS in the consecutive block. 
5.	Intra-brain activity: Based on the previous literature we expect to find some activations in frontal and temporal cortices, in areas such as precunei, PFC, ACC, superior/middle temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, caudate, or supplementary motor area. 
6.	Inter-brain activity (INS): based on the previous literature, we expect to find higher INS in TPJ, and the PFC.

Dominant task (ICG):
1.	Validation: We expect that pairs with higher INS will perform better (finish with a higher pair outcome). 
2.	Group comparison: We expect higher INS in cooperative pairs than competitive pairs. 
3.	Behavior level: Assuming that there will be differences in dominance behavior observable in siblings’ interaction, we expect to find the following: 1) More cooperative pairs will a) have fewer crashes and b) smaller difference in their number of winning trials; 2) dominate-subordinate pairs will a) have less crashes and b) a larger differences in their number of winning trials, with the dominant sibling winning more; 3) dominant-dominant pairs will have a) more crashes and b) a smaller difference in their number of winning trials. 
4.	Intra-brain activity: We expect to find higher activity during the competition (mutual-defection) than cooperative behavior in DLPFC, OFC, and temporal cortices. 
5.	Inter-brain activity: We expect to find higher and denser synchronization (more inter-brain connections) in cooperation (mutual-cooperation and tit-for-tat) trials than in defection trials. Based on the previous literature, this higher INS might be located in frontal areas such as OFC, frontopolar cortex (BA 10), superior frontal gyrus, cingulate motor area, precuneus/superior parietal lobule (BA 7), and TPJ. We also expect to find high INS in TPJ in dominant-subordinate pairs and that the direction of the synchronization goes from the dominant to the subordinate. 
6.	 We expect that subordinate individuals will describe their strategy in cooperative or fair terms while dominant individuals will describe their strategy in competition, dominance, or aggression terms (assessed by self-report questions at the end of the task). 
7.	 Questionnaires: We expect that more competitive individuals will show higher scores on the conflict and rivalry factors in the Adult Sibling Relationship Questionnaire, as well as higher scores on the Dominance, Prestige, and Leadership Scale, the Personal Development Competitive Attitude Scale, the Hypercompetitive Attitude Scale, the Personal Sense of Power Scale and on dominant leadership and ruthless self-advancement factors in the Rank Style Peers Questionnaire. 
8.	Gender: We expect brothers to show more dominant behavior than sisters. Since sex studies differ in their results, we refrain from a specific hypothesis concerning the brain area, but expect potential differences in the locations of INS characterizing male-male and female-female pairs.

Aggressive task (iTAP):
In this task we have two aims:
a)	To analyze the aggressive behavior.
1.	We expect that non-aggressive pairs will have higher synchrony than aggressive pairs. 
2.	Intra-brain activity: We expect to find the commonly reported areas during the classic TAP such as PFC, OFC, ACC, thalamus, amygdala, and insula (although there may be differences because 1) participants are having a real interaction 2) participants know each other well).  
3.	Inter-brain activity: To our knowledge, this is the first time that purely aggressive behavior will be studied using the hyperscanning technique. Based on single-person results, we might find higher INS between both non-aggressive and aggressive-aggressive pairs in different areas relevant to process the reaction to provocation and aggression (PFC, OFC, ACC, thalamus, amygdala, and insula and others, important to understand the actions of another individual such as TPJ).
4.	Gender: We expect brothers to show more aggressive behavior than sisters. Since sex studies differ in their results, we cannot make a specific hypothesis in the brain area but expect a different INS between male-male and female-female, perhaps located in different areas.

b)	Side aim: Exploring the mentalizing behavior through the rock, paper, and scissors game. 

1.	Intra-brain activity: Based on the previous literature, we expect to find activation in mentalizing areas such as PFC, anterior paracingulate cortex, precuneus, TPJ, insula, or superior/middle temporal gyrus. We also expect to find different activations related to different outcomes (win, lose and tie), as well as whether the participant sticks to their previous selection or changes their decision (e.g., in the STG or insula). 
2.	Inter-brain activity: We expect to find activation in ToM areas such as PFC, precuneus, ACC, TPJ. If we find increased INS, we expect that higher INS during the decision phase will be associated with higher INS during the outcome phase. We expect to find increased INS during win feedback.

table.study_design_overview:
The protocol of the pilot study can be found here: DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/QDEVJ

The study includes same-sex sibling pairs, with a maximum of 5 years between them and an age range from 18 to 35 years old. These pairs will be classified into two groups using the Siblings Type Questionnaire (STQ, Stewart 2001). The first group will be defined as cooperative, supportive, and intimate relationships (high mutuality, and low criticism, apathy, competition subscales), and the second group will be characterized by more conflictual, competitive, hostile, and apathetic relationships (presenting the opposite pattern in the STQ subscales). 
Sibling pairs will be measured on the same day once at the same time.

Experimental procedure
The procedure of the hyperscanning study will be carried out as follows: at the beginning of the experiment, participants will be informed about the study and all relevant procedures. We start with instructions about the study and the tasks. Subsequently, a one-hour MRI session will follow, including an initial localizer, and structural T1-weighted image acquisition. Later, they will receive further task-related instructions, and when all is understood, upon which they will be asked to complete all three computer-based tasks while a T2-weighted image is being acquired. Then, there will be a 10 minutes break. Afterward, individuals will be asked to complete several questionnaires (See Figure Time structure.png, ). Lastly, all participants will be compensated. In general, it is estimated that the experiment will last about three hours. 

Tasks designs:

Cooperation task design:
The Cooperation Tetris Task (CoTT), is a cooperative game, using the well-known Tetris game. In the original game, a descending piece must be fitted to a structure of pieces at the bottom of the playing field. During fall, the piece can be (1) moved (left / right) and (2) rotated to fit. The player wins points every time they completely filled a line with pieces. To make this game interactive, we modified the original version into a two-player scenario. Here, one player can only move and the other can only rotate the piece, which switches every block. Thus, only with the coordination and cooperation of both players is it possible to get the piece in the right position in order to fill a line. Which player moves or rotates will be selected randomly for the first block and it will switch sequentially in the next blocks. Each block will contain three easy and three complex scenarios. In easy scenarios, there is only one clear position to put the piece, while in complex scenarios there are two equally good positions to place the piece so that it creates a conflict between players. Hence, complex scenarios leave more room for leader-follower behaviors to show. In total, this task has 48 scenarios (192 trials in total), which are divided into 4 blocks. For an example of an easy and complex scenario, see figures 1 and 2 of the file “MRI task.pdf”.

Dominance task design:
As far as we know, there are no specific behavioral tasks for real-time dominance behavior and interactions. Some paradigms have studied how people behave when they are forced to adopt the role of "leader" or "subordinate", but this behavior does not come naturally. To study a real interaction it is important to let the participants make a decision and depending on that decision they will be classified as dominant or subordinate. In this sense, we suggest that the chicken game, a task that is generally used to study cooperation and competition but taking the definition of dominance written above, can also be used to study dominant and subordinate behavior. 
The Interactive Chicken Game (ICG) is a modified version of the chicken’s game. This paradigm, which is part of the game theory, creates a conflict between two players. In the original version, two cars drive towards each other until they collide. Each player is in control of one of the cars, such that they select in a matrix to turn away beforehand and yield the road to the other player. If neither player turns, they crash. This similar defection of both players and results in the worst outcome (Astolfi et al., 2010). If both the players cooperate (if both turn), they do not win any points (or have a small win). If one player turns and the other defects, the defector receives a high reward, while the cooperator receives a high loss. The payoff matrix is not fixed, thus the amount and valence of outcomes have changed across studies (De Heus, Hoogervorst, & Van Dijk, 2010). The players aim to reach the maximum score. In this version to increase interactivity in our task, we have adapted the game showing participants a video of two cars approaching (first-person driver’s perspective). Depending on the moment a player decides to turn, the reward/ loss will be different (the closer to the collision point, the higher the outcome). There is an interval of collision in which, if they cross the line, the car continues forward and a car crash cannot be avoided (defect condition). This point of non-return was set to second 5 and the crash at second 6. After the behavioral pilot test, we decided to add a decision phase consisting of a question about their intuition of what they think they will do in the next game "turn" or "continue". We tell the participants in the instructions that this has to be a quick and intuitive decision of what they plan to do, but of course, it is not the final decision, and they can change it if they feel so while driving. After that, they see a video of the cars approaching, and finally the feedback phase. This task has a total of 42 trials, divided into three blocks. To see the design of the conditions and each trial see figures 4, 6, and 7 of the file "MRI tasks.pdf".
In the classic version of this game, there is only a choice to be made between turning vs. continuing (cooperating vs. defecting), which is a binary decision, but we believe that by widening the range of decisions we can see a broader and more complex behavior (if one person is more subordinate and always turns at the beginning if there is a cooperative behavior of always turning at the same point (e.g. point 5), or how the dominant behavior emerges (lengthening the moment of the turn, always crashing, etc.).  

Aggressive task design: 
The interactive Taylor Aggression Paradigm (iTAP) is a modified version of the TAP (Taylor, 1967). In the original version, participants were told to play against an ostensible opponent in a competitive reaction time task. Participants selected the intensity of an electric shock to administer or the amount of money or points to be subtracted to the ostensible opponent in case he/she loses the trial, who ostensibly did the same for them. If the participant lost the competition round, which was preprogrammed, he/she received a shock of their opponent’s choosing (manipulating the level of provocation). The behavioral response to this provocation served as a measure for reactive aggression. 
One of the main modifications in the current study is the introduction of a second real opponent. Because of the introduction of this real second player, we have changed the following aspects:
1) Usually a competition reaction time task is used in the competition phase, but we will use the “rock, paper, and scissors game” since the competition reaction time task is less reliable if we manipulate the win/lose trials. In this well-known game, participants have to select between three options “rock”, “paper” and “scissors”. A player who decides to play rock will beat another player who has chosen scissors, but will lose to one who has played paper; a player who selected paper will lose to a play of scissors. If both participants chose the same option, none of them will win. We will use this condition as a control condition in which the provocation is ineffective. 
2) The outcome of the competition task will be pre-selected so all participants will lose, win and tie the same amount of rounds (specifically four wins, four loses, and three ties per block). The outcomes are pseudorandomized and fixed across all participants, and both receive the same outcome each trial. 
3) The money subtractions in the current version are actually chosen by the players (in contrast to the pre-selected provocations of a computer-programmed opponent in the original paradigms). The only manipulation that will be made to induce a conflict situation is the manipulation of the first five trials in the second block (both will see that their partner provoked them). We have pre-set the provocation values starting at 30, 50, 50, 60, and 70 cents for all participants (this way everyone will start the block with a medium-high provocation).
4) We include a non-aggressive option because this is one of the main criticisms of the original task (Tedeschi, & Quigley, 1996) so that participants are "forced" to select between the options of the low, medium, or high aggressiveness. However, in our task, there is a non-aggressive option (select 0), which assures us that if the participant chooses a low, medium, or high aggression option, it is done voluntarily and not because they had no other option.
This task consists of 33 trials, divided into three blocks (non-provocation, post-manipulation, recovery blocks). Each block has 11 trials, and between the first and second block, there will be five manipulated trials. To see the design of each trial see figure 8 of the file "MRI tasks.pdf".
All measurements will be conducted via the clinic’s own 3T scanners. A virtual server is hosted at the Brain Imaging Facility to handle any communication for the hyperscanning platform. Experimental paradigms are synchronized by having the paradigm-presenting computers located at the respective fMRI scanners (hereafter referred to as “client”) communicate with this server over TCP/IP. These clients will send paradigm-relevant information like “readiness” and trial information to the server. Upon receiving specific messages from both clients the server replies to both clients with an appropriate message. Contrary to starting the experimental paradigm based on a scanner trigger, as is common practice, the paradigms will send a trigger signal over a parallel port to start the prepared MRI sequence. This ensures that both scanners are synchronized with a maximum latency of approximately 16 milliseconds. To see how each task is synchronized see figures 2, 5, and 9 from the “MRI task.pdf” file.

table.randomization:
The order of the paradigms is fixed for all participants.
In the Cooperative Tetris task, the scenarios have been randomly arranged to each block and will be displayed following always the same order to participants (easy-complex-easy-complex-easy-complex).
In the Interactive Chicken Game, videos will be displayed randomly (simple randomization) throughout the blocks. 
In the Interactive TAP, the feedback order has been already randomly arranged and will be shown in the same order for all participants.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
Inclusion criteria are to be a pair of siblings of the same sex, within an age range of 18-35 years, and a maximum difference of five years between them. All participants have normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
Exclusion criteria: Any neurological abnormalities, psychotic symptoms, mental illness, or substance-related disorders that may impair cognitive function, as well as any MRI contraindications (such as metal in the body, pregnancy, or intrauterine device, among others). 
The present study will recruit 40 sibling pairs, all of them will be healthy controls.
Same-sex siblings will be recruited through flyers (containing information about the study, including inclusion and exclusion criteria, study duration, and participation rates). These flyers will be posted in local shops in Aachen (Germany), as well as through Internet forums and social media such as Facebook. 
All individuals will receive the same amount of €60 after the experiment. 
During the recruitment phase, participants will fill out a recruitment questionnaire with demographic data and the Sibling Type Questionnaire (STQ) followed by oral screening and information procedures. 
Participants who do not fit our criteria will be excluded. 
Based on the STQ scores, participants will be classified into two groups (cooperative and conflictual siblings). The cooperative group will include pairs with high mutuality, low criticism, low apathy, low competition. The conflictual group will include pairs with the opposite pattern.
table.sample_size:
The sample size will be about 40 sibling pairs (80 participants). The final sample will be determined by the time for the study and the financial support.
The previous study is planned to recruit 20 pairs for the behavioral pilot study to test all the tasks (we have already measured 14 of the 20 pairs).
table.sample_size_rationale:
Few studies investigated social interaction with the fMRI hyperscanning technique. Based on recent similar studies, the sample sizes range from 17 pairs (Koike et al., 2019), 19 pairs (Abe et al., 2019), 43 pairs (Tomlin, Nedic, Prentice, Holmes, & Cohen, 2013) to 48 pairs (Koike et al., 2016). Since we aim to have a powerful sample, while at the same time including a relatively homogeneous group of healthy participants, we think that, based on the numbers included in prior studies, 40 pairs seem an appropriate size for studying social interaction between siblings with fMRI hyperscanning. 
Moreover, the sample size of 40 pairs was also reached because of the availability of funds, time, and recruitment constraints.
table.stopping_rule: We will stop measuring in September 2023 due to time constraints.
table.manipulated_variables:
In the cooperative Tetris task, we manipulate the difficulty of trials. The two levels of this variable are easy (1) and complex (2) scenarios.  
In the interactive chicken game, there is no active experimental manipulation. The experiment is thus a natural observation of the behavior of each sibling pair. 
In the interactive TAP, we manipulate the level of provocation for the first trials of the second block. In the first block the provocation will not be manipulated (we will let them decide the level of punishment), but in the first five trials of the second block, the provocation will be manipulated.
table.measured_variables:
In the cooperation Tetris task, cooperative behavior will be measured by the number of deleted lines, as well as leadership behavior, which will be obtained by calculating who makes the first move more often. We will also measure the feedback siblings give to each other by selecting between three statements (positive, neutral, or negative). Moreover, brain activity will be measured using the BOLD signal.
We will measure the individual success (number of deleted lines) per individual and pair. We will also measure the efficiency per individual and pair. Efficiency is defined as the ratio between how many movements the person/partner needed to delete a line and how many were the minimum necessary to accomplish that action. In this way we are not only looking at whether or not they were able to delete a line each trial but how effective they were in doing so. We expect that the more coordinated (and therefore more synchronized) pairs will have both high success and efficiency ratios.
After each block, some questions will be asked to assess personal success, responsibility for overall performance, shared mental representation, leadership, and teamwork. At the end of the task, we will ask them how much they liked the task, how difficult it was, and how often they play Tetris. 
In the interactive chicken game, dominance behavior will be measured by the participant's decisions, which can be to turn or to go ahead (in the intuition question and while driving). Reaction time is defined as the time it takes for participants to press the turn/continue button in the intuition question and when the participant decides to turn while driving will also be measured. We also measure if the participant presses after the point of non-return. After each block, some questions will be asked to assess responsibility for the outcome, personal motivation and to rate how much some statements represent how they felt when they won or lost a trial. In addition, participants will receive feedback on who won, who lost the previous block, or if they tied. Some questions about his/her and his/her sibling's behavioral intentions and strategy during the game will be asked at the end of the task. Moreover, brain activity will be measured using the BOLD signal.
In the interactive Taylor Aggression Paradigm (iTAP) - aggressive behavior will be measured by the amount of money that participants select to be subtracted from their sibling in the decision phase (from 0 to 90), and the aggression level in trial x serves as the provocation level in trial x + 1 to the other sibling. This interdependence is tested statistically. Furthermore, brain activity will be measured using the BOLD signal.
After each block, some questions will be asked to assess personal motivation, aggressive intentions, fairness emotion, and to rate how much some statements represent how they felt when they won or lost a trial. In addition, participants will receive feedback on who won, who lost the previous block, or if they tied. Some questions about his/her and his/her sibling's behavioral intentions and strategy during the game will be asked at the end of the task. 
Demographics: Participants will report their current age, socio-economic level, level of education, current romantic relationship status, handedness, and some questions about their relationship with their parents during their childhood. 
Questionnaires:
1. Sibling Type Questionnaire (STQ; Stewart, 2001): this questionnaire is assessed during the recruitment phase to classify the participants. It is a self-report questionnaire with 50 items that assess mutuality, criticism, apathy, competition, and longing factors in a sibling relationship. 
2. Aggression Questionnaire (AG; Buss, & Perry, 1992): 29-items scale based on the ranking of statements along a 5-point continuum from "extremely uncharacteristic of me" to "extremely characteristic of me", yielding 4 factors: Physical Aggression, Verbal Aggression, Anger, and Hostility. 
3. Adult Sibling Relationship Questionnaire (ASRQ; Stocker, Lanthier, & Furman, 1997): 81-items scale spread over 14 subscales that assess the qualitative features of sibling relationships in adults. 
4. Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11; Patton, Stanford, & Barratt, 1995): 30-items on a 4-point scale that assesses impulsive behaviors and preferences. 
5. Dominance, prestige, and leadership scale (DoPL; Suessenbach, Loughnan, Schönbrodt, Moore, & Back, 2019): 18-items on a 6-point scale that assesses social power motives, specifically desires for dominance, prestige, and leadership. 
6. Personal Development Competitive Attitude Scale (PDCA; Ryckman, Hammer, Kaczor, & Gold, 1996): the 15-items scale that assesses the desire to improve our own personal performance or "competing to excel". 
7. Hypercompetitive Attitude Scale (HCA; Ryckman, Hammer, Kaczor, & Gold, 1990): the 26-items scale that assesses the desire to have a better performance than the other, or "competing to win".  
8. Machiavellianism Scale (Mach IV; Christie, & Geis, 1970): 20-items self-report measure of Machiavellianism. 
9. State-Trait Anger Expression Inventory (STAXI; Spielberger, 2010): the 57-items scale that assesses the intensity of anger as an emotional state (State Anger) and the disposition to experience angry feelings as a personality trait (Trait Anger).
10. Rank Style with Peers Questionnaire (RSPQ; Zuroff, Fournier, Patall, & Leybman, 2010): 17-items scale subdivided into 3 subscales that assess the interaction style people typically use to maintain or improve social standing among peers. 
11. Personal Sense of Power scale (Anderson, John, & Keltner, 2012): 8-items on a 7-points scale that assesses the personal sense of power in a given relationship. 
12. NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI; McCrae, & Costa Jr, 2004): the 60-items scale that evaluates personality traits divided into subcategories such as Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness.
table.indices:
For the CoTT, we will take the average cooperative performance per block and across the entire task (defined as the number of deleted lines) to create a single measure of cooperative behavior per block and sibling pair. 
For the other tasks, we will first model the behavior trial-by trial on the individual level and the dual (sibling) level. As the individual responses within the dyad are unlikely to be independent but influenced by the characteristics of the other member, interdependence between the individual responses is assumed (which prevents significance bias). Since commonly used statistical procedures assume independent observations, and we cannot assume this independence, it is necessary to treat the dyad rather than the individual as the unit of the analysis. The Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM: Kashy & Kenny, 1999; Kenny, 1996) is designed to measure interdependence within interpersonal relationships because takes into account interdependencies by measuring associations between scores within the dyad and assessing the extent to which each member of the dyad influences the responses of the other member (Fitzpatrick, Gareau, Lafontaine, & Gaudreau, 2016). In this model, individual measures are treated as being nested within the dyad.
table.statistical_tests:
Overall, statistical analyses will be performed using IBM SPSS Statistics Version 25.0 (IBM; Armonk, New York, USA).

Differences in demographic characteristics, such as age, sex, and educational background in participants will be determined using independent-samples t-tests. 
For further information about the behavioral analyses, you can consult the analysis plan described in the previous registration (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/QDEVJ). 

Intra-brain activity analysis and seed region selection:
We will examine brain responses to task conditions in a classical general linear convolution model (GLM) and independent component analysis (ICA) to select regions of interest and extract time series for subsequent connectivity analysis. ICA is a data-driven blind source separation approach, which extracts the underlying, maximally independent sources (components) from a multivariate data set. By analyzing fMRI data in a model-free and hypothesis-free manner, the nonlinear and unpredictable dynamic of social interactions can be more appropriately captured. 

Our plan is to use both theoretical regions of interest to start our analyses, as well as the brain regions we obtain with ICA. The reasoning behind this is that, although there is similar literature that can guide us about which brain areas to look at, as the study tasks have not been used previously in MRI, we cannot be sure that we are looking at the relevant areas. Thus, we aim to identify these areas first in a data driven approach. 
In the same direction of reasoning, we have selected different methods of analysis that we could use depending on the data, we will be dealing with, and whether it is possible to use such a model.

The possible analysis approaches are: 
1.	Interpersonal brain-behavior dependencies (iBBDs): Capturing the brain responses of one individual which are modulated by, or depend on, the behavior of an interaction partner iBBDs model was created. In this model, brain signals that are elicited as a direct response to their interaction partner’s previous behavior are identified by an event-related model of each individual's brain activity in a short period following each of their partner’s movements. For previous application in fMRI hyperscanning, see Špiláková, Shaw, Czekóová, & Brázdil, (2019).
2.	Inter-subject correlation (ISC) analysis: ISC analyses are carried out to investigate whether the time-course of brain signals within these patterns are correlated or aligned between interactive pairs. ISC can be quantified using Pearson’s correlation coefficients between the time series of a given ROI between the two subjects. For previous application in fMRI hyperscanning, see Špiláková, Shaw, Czekóová, Mareček, & Brázdil, (2020) and Xie et al., (2020)
3.	Actor-partner Independence Model (APIM): This model is designed to measure interdependence within interpersonal relationships because takes into account interdependencies by measuring associations between scores within the dyad and assessing the extent to which each member of the dyad influences the responses of the other member. In this model, individual measures are treated as being nested within the dyad. For example, if sibling A shows higher dominant behavior (defined as holding longer without turning) in the previous trial, this may influence his/ her next decision (actor effect) and the other’s decision (partner effect). We can include brain synchronization in this model by defining it as a possible moderator of the actor or partner effects. We will perform all tests using structural equation modeling and multilevel modeling. For further information, see Kashy & Kenny, 1999; Kenny, 1996, Fitzpatrick, Gareau, Lafontaine, & Gaudreau, 2016.
4.	Dynamical causal modeling (DCM): In this model, instead of using BOLD responses, the effects of the level of the neural population are used. The effective connectivity (instead of the correlation between time series) is examined, as well as the direction of this connectivity between those brain regions. For each pair, a DCM model is specified taking ROIs as seed regions. For previous application in fMRI hyperscanning, see Bilek (2020). 

We will use the following analysis time-windows:
CoTT:
All brain activity will be included for intra- and inter-brain analysis during the scenarios, separated by a waiting phase between mini-blocks.
ICG:
For the inter-brain activity analysis we will first look for synchronization in:
a)	Decision-making during the driving phase (interactive car game).
b)	Decision-making as a combination between the intuition question phase and driving phase. 
iTAP:
We will separately analyze synchronization in: 
a)	Aggressive behavior: The money decision & provocation feedback.
b)	Mentalizing behavior: rock-paper-scissors decision & outcome feedback. 
For all the analysis approaches, we will use permutation tests to compare really interacting pairs to those of randomly composed non-pairs. Fake pairs are created by matching individuals from one pair with those who have performed the same task (and with the same and the opposite role, if possible). For example, by matching one person with the rotation role of pair A, and one person with the movement role of pair B). table.transformations: fMRI: After removal of the first three fMRI volumes, functional scans are realigned to the first volume of the remaining, co-registered to the T1 image, normalized to a standard template (MNI), and spatially smoothed with an 8×8×8 mm full-width at half-maximum Gaussian kernel. A high-pass filter with a cut-off of 128s is applied.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p<0.05 criteria for determining if t-test or ANOVA results are significantly different from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct. All second-level statistics are corrected for multiple comparisons with an extent family-wise error (FWE) corrected cluster level threshold at p<0.05 (a voxel-wise threshold at uncorrected p<0.001).
table.data_exclusion_criteria: If a participant does not respond to any of the trials, the participant will be excluded.
table.missing_data_handling: If a participant does not respond to any of the trials, the participant will be excluded.
table.exploratory_analyses:
We will calculate the correlation between the team performance and the degree of observed INS across participants within each pair. Finally, we will do some exploratory correlation analyses between behavioral measures (e.g. average aggression), questionnaires data (e.g. AQ total score), and selected brain regions (e.g. PFC). 
Outcome variables of the three tasks may also be related to each other.

The study includes same-sex sibling pairs, with a maximum of 5 years between them and an age range from 18 to 35 years old. These pairs will be classified into two groups using the Siblings Type Questionnaire (STQ, Stewart 2001). The first group will be defined as cooperative, supportive, and intimate relationships (high mutuality, and low criticism, apathy, competition subscales), and the second group will be characterized by more conflictual, competitive, hostile, and apathetic relationships (presenting the opposite pattern in the STQ subscales).
Sibling pairs will be measured on the same day once at the same time.

Experimental procedure
The procedure of the hyperscanning study will be carried out as follows: at the beginning of the experiment, participants will be informed about the study and all relevant procedures. We start with instructions about the study and the tasks. Subsequently, a one-hour MRI session will follow, including an initial localizer, and structural T1-weighted image acquisition. Later, they will receive further task-related instructions, and when all is understood, upon which they will be asked to complete all three computer-based tasks while a T2-weighted image is being acquired. Then, there will be a 10 minutes break. Afterward, individuals will be asked to complete several questionnaires (See Figure Time structure.png, ). Lastly, all participants will be compensated. In general, it is estimated that the experiment will last about three hours.

Tasks designs:

Cooperation task design:
The Cooperation Tetris Task (CoTT), is a cooperative game, using the well-known Tetris game. In the original game, a descending piece must be fitted to a structure of pieces at the bottom of the playing field. During fall, the piece can be (1) moved (left / right) and (2) rotated to fit. The player wins points every time they completely filled a line with pieces. To make this game interactive, we modified the original version into a two-player scenario. Here, one player can only move and the other can only rotate the piece, which switches every block. Thus, only with the coordination and cooperation of both players is it possible to get the piece in the right position in order to fill a line. Which player moves or rotates will be selected randomly for the first block and it will switch sequentially in the next blocks. Each block will contain three easy and three complex scenarios. In easy scenarios, there is only one clear position to put the piece, while in complex scenarios there are two equally good positions to place the piece so that it creates a conflict between players. Hence, complex scenarios leave more room for leader-follower behaviors to show. In total, this task has 48 scenarios (192 trials in total), which are divided into 4 blocks. For an example of an easy and complex scenario, see figures 1 and 2 of the file “MRI task.pdf”.

Dominance task design:
As far as we know, there are no specific behavioral tasks for real-time dominance behavior and interactions. Some paradigms have studied how people behave when they are forced to adopt the role of \"leader\" or \"subordinate\", but this behavior does not come naturally. To study a real interaction it is important to let the participants make a decision and depending on that decision they will be classified as dominant or subordinate. In this sense, we suggest that the chicken game, a task that is generally used to study cooperation and competition but taking the definition of dominance written above, can also be used to study dominant and subordinate behavior.
The Interactive Chicken Game (ICG) is a modified version of the chicken’s game. This paradigm, which is part of the game theory, creates a conflict between two players. In the original version, two cars drive towards each other until they collide. Each player is in control of one of the cars, such that they select in a matrix to turn away beforehand and yield the road to the other player. If neither player turns, they crash. This similar defection of both players and results in the worst outcome (Astolfi et al., 2010). If both the players cooperate (if both turn), they do not win any points (or have a small win). If one player turns and the other defects, the defector receives a high reward, while the cooperator receives a high loss. The payoff matrix is not fixed, thus the amount and valence of outcomes have changed across studies (De Heus, Hoogervorst, & Van Dijk, 2010). The players aim to reach the maximum score. In this version to increase interactivity in our task, we have adapted the game showing participants a video of two cars approaching (first-person driver’s perspective). Depending on the moment a player decides to turn, the reward/ loss will be different (the closer to the collision point, the higher the outcome). There is an interval of collision in which, if they cross the line, the car continues forward and a car crash cannot be avoided (defect condition). This point of non-return was set to second 5 and the crash at second 6. After the behavioral pilot test, we decided to add a decision phase consisting of a question about their intuition of what they think they will do in the next game \"turn\" or \"continue\". We tell the participants in the instructions that this has to be a quick and intuitive decision of what they plan to do, but of course, it is not the final decision, and they can change it if they feel so while driving. After that, they see a video of the cars approaching, and finally the feedback phase. This task has a total of 42 trials, divided into three blocks. To see the design of the conditions and each trial see figures 4, 6, and 7 of the file \"MRI tasks.pdf\".
In the classic version of this game, there is only a choice to be made between turning vs. continuing (cooperating vs. defecting), which is a binary decision, but we believe that by widening the range of decisions we can see a broader and more complex behavior (if one person is more subordinate and always turns at the beginning if there is a cooperative behavior of always turning at the same point (e.g. point 5), or how the dominant behavior emerges (lengthening the moment of the turn, always crashing, etc.).

Aggressive task design:
The interactive Taylor Aggression Paradigm (iTAP) is a modified version of the TAP (Taylor, 1967). In the original version, participants were told to play against an ostensible opponent in a competitive reaction time task. Participants selected the intensity of an electric shock to administer or the amount of money or points to be subtracted to the ostensible opponent in case he/she loses the trial, who ostensibly did the same for them. If the participant lost the competition round, which was preprogrammed, he/she received a shock of their opponent’s choosing (manipulating the level of provocation). The behavioral response to this provocation served as a measure for reactive aggression.
One of the main modifications in the current study is the introduction of a second real opponent. Because of the introduction of this real second player, we have changed the following aspects:
1) Usually a competition reaction time task is used in the competition phase, but we will use the “rock, paper, and scissors game” since the competition reaction time task is less reliable if we manipulate the win/lose trials. In this well-known game, participants have to select between three options “rock”, “paper” and “scissors”. A player who decides to play rock will beat another player who has chosen scissors, but will lose to one who has played paper; a player who selected paper will lose to a play of scissors. If both participants chose the same option, none of them will win. We will use this condition as a control condition in which the provocation is ineffective.
2) The outcome of the competition task will be pre-selected so all participants will lose, win and tie the same amount of rounds (specifically four wins, four loses, and three ties per block). The outcomes are pseudorandomized and fixed across all participants, and both receive the same outcome each trial.
3) The money subtractions in the current version are actually chosen by the players (in contrast to the pre-selected provocations of a computer-programmed opponent in the original paradigms). The only manipulation that will be made to induce a conflict situation is the manipulation of the first five trials in the second block (both will see that their partner provoked them). We have pre-set the provocation values starting at 30, 50, 50, 60, and 70 cents for all participants (this way everyone will start the block with a medium-high provocation).
4) We include a non-aggressive option because this is one of the main criticisms of the original task (Tedeschi, & Quigley, 1996) so that participants are \"forced\" to select between the options of the low, medium, or high aggressiveness. However, in our task, there is a non-aggressive option (select 0), which assures us that if the participant chooses a low, medium, or high aggression option, it is done voluntarily and not because they had no other option.
This task consists of 33 trials, divided into three blocks (non-provocation, post-manipulation, recovery blocks). Each block has 11 trials, and between the first and second block, there will be five manipulated trials. To see the design of each trial see figure 8 of the file \"MRI tasks.pdf\".
All measurements will be conducted via the clinic’s own 3T scanners. A virtual server is hosted at the Brain Imaging Facility to handle any communication for the hyperscanning platform. Experimental paradigms are synchronized by having the paradigm-presenting computers located at the respective fMRI scanners (hereafter referred to as “client”) communicate with this server over TCP/IP. These clients will send paradigm-relevant information like “readiness” and trial information to the server. Upon receiving specific messages from both clients the server replies to both clients with an appropriate message. Contrary to starting the experimental paradigm based on a scanner trigger, as is common practice, the paradigms will send a trigger signal over a parallel port to start the prepared MRI sequence. This ensures that both scanners are synchronized with a maximum latency of approximately 16 milliseconds. To see how each task is synchronized see figures 2, 5, and 9 from the “MRI task.pdf” file.

Demographics: Participants will report their current age, socio-economic level, level of education, current romantic relationship status, handedness, and some questions about their relationship with their parents during their childhood.
Questionnaires:
1. Sibling Type Questionnaire (STQ; Stewart, 2001): this questionnaire is assessed during the recruitment phase to classify the participants. It is a self-report questionnaire with 50 items that assess mutuality, criticism, apathy, competition, and longing factors in a sibling relationship.
2. Aggression Questionnaire (AG; Buss, & Perry, 1992): 29-items scale based on the ranking of statements along a 5-point continuum from \"extremely uncharacteristic of me\" to \"extremely characteristic of me\", yielding 4 factors: Physical Aggression, Verbal Aggression, Anger, and Hostility.
3. Adult Sibling Relationship Questionnaire (ASRQ; Stocker, Lanthier, & Furman, 1997): 81-items scale spread over 14 subscales that assess the qualitative features of sibling relationships in adults.
4. Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11; Patton, Stanford, & Barratt, 1995): 30-items on a 4-point scale that assesses impulsive behaviors and preferences.
5. Dominance, prestige, and leadership scale (DoPL; Suessenbach, Loughnan, Schönbrodt, Moore, & Back, 2019): 18-items on a 6-point scale that assesses social power motives, specifically desires for dominance, prestige, and leadership.
6. Personal Development Competitive Attitude Scale (PDCA; Ryckman, Hammer, Kaczor, & Gold, 1996): the 15-items scale that assesses the desire to improve our own personal performance or \"competing to excel\".
7. Hypercompetitive Attitude Scale (HCA; Ryckman, Hammer, Kaczor, & Gold, 1990): the 26-items scale that assesses the desire to have a better performance than the other, or \"competing to win\".
8. Machiavellianism Scale (Mach IV; Christie, & Geis, 1970): 20-items self-report measure of Machiavellianism.
9. State-Trait Anger Expression Inventory (STAXI; Spielberger, 2010): the 57-items scale that assesses the intensity of anger as an emotional state (State Anger) and the disposition to experience angry feelings as a personality trait (Trait Anger).
10. Rank Style with Peers Questionnaire (RSPQ; Zuroff, Fournier, Patall, & Leybman, 2010): 17-items scale subdivided into 3 subscales that assess the interaction style people typically use to maintain or improve social standing among peers.
11. Personal Sense of Power scale (Anderson, John, & Keltner, 2012): 8-items on a 7-points scale that assesses the personal sense of power in a given relationship.
12. NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI; McCrae, & Costa Jr, 2004): the 60-items scale that evaluates personality traits divided into subcategories such as Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness.", "For the CoTT, we will take the average cooperative performance per block and across the entire task (defined as the number of deleted lines) to create a single measure of cooperative behavior per block and sibling pair.
For the other tasks, we will first model the behavior trial-by trial on the individual level and the dual (sibling) level. As the individual responses within the dyad are unlikely to be independent but influenced by the characteristics of the other member, interdependence between the individual responses is assumed (which prevents significance bias). Since commonly used statistical procedures assume independent observations, and we cannot assume this independence, it is necessary to treat the dyad rather than the individual as the unit of the analysis. The Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM: Kashy & Kenny, 1999; Kenny, 1996) is designed to measure interdependence within interpersonal relationships because takes into account interdependencies by measuring associations between scores within the dyad and assessing the extent to which each member of the dyad influences the responses of the other member (Fitzpatrick, Gareau, Lafontaine, & Gaudreau, 2016). In this model, individual measures are treated as being nested within the dyad.", "Overall, statistical analyses will be performed using IBM SPSS Statistics Version 25.0 (IBM; Armonk, New York, USA).

Differences in demographic characteristics, such as age, sex, and educational background in participants will be determined using independent-samples t-tests.
For further information about the behavioral analyses, you can consult the analysis plan described in the previous registration (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/QDEVJ).

Intra-brain activity analysis and seed region selection:
We will examine brain responses to task conditions in a classical general linear convolution model (GLM) and independent component analysis (ICA) to select regions of interest and extract time series for subsequent connectivity analysis. ICA is a data-driven blind source separation approach, which extracts the underlying, maximally independent sources (components) from a multivariate data set. By analyzing fMRI data in a model-free and hypothesis-free manner, the nonlinear and unpredictable dynamic of social interactions can be more appropriately captured.

Our plan is to use both theoretical regions of interest to start our analyses, as well as the brain regions we obtain with ICA. The reasoning behind this is that, although there is similar literature that can guide us about which brain areas to look at, as the study tasks have not been used previously in MRI, we cannot be sure that we are looking at the relevant areas. Thus, we aim to identify these areas first in a data driven approach.
In the same direction of reasoning, we have selected different methods of analysis that we could use depending on the data, we will be dealing with, and whether it is possible to use such a model.

The possible analysis approaches are:
1.\tInterpersonal brain-behavior dependencies (iBBDs): Capturing the brain responses of one individual which are modulated by, or depend on, the behavior of an interaction partner iBBDs model was created. In this model, brain signals that are elicited as a direct response to their interaction partner’s previous behavior are identified by an event-related model of each individual's brain activity in a short period following each of their partner’s movements. For previous application in fMRI hyperscanning, see Špiláková, Shaw, Czekóová, & Brázdil, (2019).
2.\tInter-subject correlation (ISC) analysis: ISC analyses are carried out to investigate whether the time-course of brain signals within these patterns are correlated or aligned between interactive pairs. ISC can be quantified using Pearson’s correlation coefficients between the time series of a given ROI between the two subjects. For previous application in fMRI hyperscanning, see Špiláková, Shaw, Czekóová, Mareček, & Brázdil, (2020) and Xie et al., (2020)
3.\tActor-partner Independence Model (APIM): This model is designed to measure interdependence within interpersonal relationships because takes into account interdependencies by measuring associations between scores within the dyad and assessing the extent to which each member of the dyad influences the responses of the other member. In this model, individual measures are treated as being nested within the dyad. For example, if sibling A shows higher dominant behavior (defined as holding longer without turning) in the previous trial, this may influence his/ her next decision (actor effect) and the other’s decision (partner effect). We can include brain synchronization in this model by defining it as a possible moderator of the actor or partner effects. We will perform all tests using structural equation modeling and multilevel modeling. For further information, see Kashy & Kenny, 1999; Kenny, 1996, Fitzpatrick, Gareau, Lafontaine, & Gaudreau, 2016.
4.\tDynamical causal modeling (DCM): In this model, instead of using BOLD responses, the effects of the level of the neural population are used. The effective connectivity (instead of the correlation between time series) is examined, as well as the direction of this connectivity between those brain regions. For each pair, a DCM model is specified taking ROIs as seed regions. For previous application in fMRI hyperscanning, see Bilek (2020).

We will use the following analysis time-windows:
CoTT:
All brain activity will be included for intra- and inter-brain analysis during the scenarios, separated by a waiting phase between mini-blocks.
ICG:
For the inter-brain activity analysis we will first look for synchronization in:
a)\tDecision-making during the driving phase (interactive car game).
b)\tDecision-making as a combination between the intuition question phase and driving phase.
iTAP:
We will separately analyze synchronization in:
a)\tAggressive behavior: The money decision & provocation feedback.
b)\tMentalizing behavior: rock-paper-scissors decision & outcome feedback.
For all the analysis approaches, we will use permutation tests to compare really interacting pairs to those of randomly composed non-pairs. Fake pairs are created by matching individuals from one pair with those who have performed the same task (and with the same and the opposite role, if possible). For example, by matching one person with the rotation role of pair A, and one person with the movement role of pair B). With these analyses, we ensure that the results are due to the real interaction. 61517817ec788500a640f925 Analysis plan.PNG https://osf.io/project/5jbk8/files/osfstorage/61517817ec788500a640f925 https://osf.io/download/61517817ec788500a640f925 189c34b71a76f8e63a97f3cf4e26248727e88a1344d47bff7f22e903af2fc3a4", "fMRI: After removal of the first three fMRI volumes, functional scans are realigned to the first volume of the remaining, co-registered to the T1 image, normalized to a standard template (MNI), and spatially smoothed with an 8×8×8 mm full-width at half-maximum Gaussian kernel. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 821 columns across 5 data files.
#### Issues Identified
3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("conditions.sav", "individual data.sav", "pair_data.sav"), Column = c("filter_$", "filter_$", "filter_$" ), Issues = c("🧮 SPSS filter variable — SPSS \"Select Cases\" filter variable: 43 of 50 rows are selected (va...", "🧮 SPSS filter variable — SPSS \"Select Cases\" filter variable: 95 of 100 rows are selected (v...", "🧮 SPSS filter variable — SPSS \"Select Cases\" filter variable: 46 of 50 rows are selected (va..." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding

31 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **16 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

live_data_statements: Although the single-brain approach has considerably advanced our knowledge of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying social cognition, a major limitation is that participants are not actively involved in real-time social interactions (Czeszumski et al., 2022; Schilbach & Redcay, 2025).
To confirm this latter criterion, participants were screened using the short version of the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID IV; Wittchen et al., 1997).
Participants were then interviewed by a psychologist, if necessary, to verify their suitability for the study.
Participants were recruited through flyers in university buildings and social media platforms.

After voluntary written informed consent was obtained, participants received verbal instructions about the study and task instructions using pre-recorded videos to ensure consistency of instructions across pairs.
Participants were not allowed to communicate during the task instructions in order to prevent any prior coordination.
Following the scanner session, participants completed self-report questionnaires using the "Sosci survey" online platform (https://www.soscisurvey.de/).
Participants completed all blocks in the same order, as preregistered.
It is possible that during easy blocks, participants were similarly thinking about their partner's intentions and actions.
Two participants are simultaneously scanned, and task activity is synchronized through a server.

text.text: Siblings typically represent the longest-lasting social relationships.
Second-person neuroscience provides a framework for studying the neural mechanisms of real-time, reciprocal social interactions.
Yet, most studies have focused on simplified coordination tasks, limited brain regions, and did not investigate neural dynamics between siblings.

In the first study investigating brain synchrony between siblings to date, we used fMRI hyperscanning to simultaneously record brain activity in 50 same-sex healthy young adult sibling pairs while they played a complex collaborative problem-solving Tetris game requiring continuous non-verbal complementary coordination.
Brain synchrony was quantified using inter-subject correlation across 36 regions of interest (ROIs) of the social brain atlas.
The interacting sibling pairs showed significantly higher brain synchrony than randomly permuted non-sibling pairs in 19 ROIs (FDR-corrected p < .05).
text.formatted: The interacting sibling pairs showed significantly higher brain synchrony than randomly permuted non-sibling pairs in 19 ROIs (FDR-corrected p < .05).

text.text: These regions were primarily located within the higher-level theory of mind subnetwork (including bilateral temporo-parietal junction, precuneus and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex), and intermediate-level subnetwork (including anterior insula, inferior frontal gyrus).

Greater synchrony in the left temporo-parietal junction significantly predicted better cooperative performance, suggesting that shared neural modelling of a partner's intentions supports effective collaboration.

Synchrony in frontal and temporal regions was weakly modulated by cooperative and competitive sibling relationship characteristics; however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously (uncorr. p < .05).
text.formatted: Synchrony in frontal and temporal regions was weakly modulated by cooperative and competitive sibling relationship characteristics; however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously (uncorr. p < .05).

text.text: This study provides first evidence that real-time cooperation between siblings is supported by inter-brain synchrony in core social brain networks.
We highlight the value of ecologically valid hyperscanning approaches for investigating neural mechanisms of cooperation in long-term relationships, advancing the field of relational neuroscience.
Interpersonal coordination is present at every level of social engagement in daily life (Mu et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Interpersonal coordination is present at every level of social engagement in daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Mu et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Cooperation (also referred to as collaboration or coordination), is a type of complex social interaction, involving two or more individuals coordinating their actions, attention, and mental states to achieve a shared goal (Mu et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Cooperation (also referred to as collaboration or coordination), is a type of complex social interaction, involving two or more individuals coordinating their actions, attention, and mental states to achieve a shared goal <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Mu et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Xie et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This ability involves continuously anticipating, predicting and considering one's partner's actions in order to adapt one's own behavior (Abe et al., 2019; Hakim et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This ability involves continuously anticipating, predicting and considering one's partner's actions in order to adapt one's own behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abe et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hakim et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these processes rely on the attribution of independent mental states such as intentions and desires to others, known as mentalizing (Quesque et al., 2024) or Theory of Mind (ToM; Frith & Frith, 2006).
text.formatted: Together, these processes rely on the attribution of independent mental states such as intentions and desires to others, known as mentalizing <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Quesque et al., 2024)</ref> or Theory of Mind (ToM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Frith & Frith, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Over the last decades, most of the existing neuroimaging research has relied on a single-brain approach with static, pre-recorded social stimuli to investigate processes involving ToM abilities (Czeszumski et al., 2022; Schilbach & Redcay, 2025; Xie et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Over the last decades, most of the existing neuroimaging research has relied on a single-brain approach with static, pre-recorded social stimuli to investigate processes involving ToM abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Czeszumski et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Schilbach & Redcay, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Xie et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analytic evidence from these single-brain studies has shown that the ToM network comprises the bilateral temporoparietal junction (TPJ), medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), middle temporal gyri, temporal poles, and precuneus (Alcalá-López et al., 2018; Molenberghs et al., 2016; Schurz et al., 2014; Van Overwalle, 2009).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic evidence from these single-brain studies has shown that the ToM network comprises the bilateral temporoparietal junction (TPJ), medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), middle temporal gyri, temporal poles, and precuneus <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alcalá-López et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Molenberghs et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Schurz et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Van Overwalle, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, no specific brain region or network is exclusively devoted to social processes (Alcalá-López et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Yet, no specific brain region or network is exclusively devoted to social processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alcalá-López et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Although the single-brain approach has considerably advanced our knowledge of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying social cognition, a major limitation is that participants are not actively involved in real-time social interactions (Czeszumski et al., 2022; Schilbach & Redcay, 2025).
text.formatted: Although the single-brain approach has considerably advanced our knowledge of the neurobiological mechanisms underlying social cognition, a major limitation is that participants are not actively involved in real-time social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Czeszumski et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Schilbach & Redcay, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, bidirectional interactions and continuous adaptation, which are evident in daily cooperation, are entirely missing (Xie et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Consequently, bidirectional interactions and continuous adaptation, which are evident in daily cooperation, are entirely missing <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Xie et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, there has been a recent shift toward a second-person approach (Redcay et al., 2019; Schilbach & Redcay, 2025) and what has been termed relational neuroscience (De Felice et al., 2025).
text.formatted: As a result, there has been a recent shift toward a second-person approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Redcay et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Schilbach & Redcay, 2025)</ref> and what has been termed relational neuroscience <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(De Felice et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Second-person neuroscience focuses on investigating real-time social interactions across interacting brains using hyperscanning, i.e., the simultaneous recording of brain activity between two or more interacting individuals (Czeszumski et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Second-person neuroscience focuses on investigating real-time social interactions across interacting brains using hyperscanning, i.e., the simultaneous recording of brain activity between two or more interacting individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Czeszumski et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This approach allows for the measurement of inter-brain synchrony (IBS) between interacting individuals.
IBS has become of special interest in relational neuroscience.

It is widely proposed that IBS underlies shared social experiences (De Felice et al., 2025), coordinated behavior and successful interpersonal communication (Czeszumski et al., 2022; Schilbach & Redcay, 2025; Xie et al., 2020).
text.formatted: It is widely proposed that IBS underlies shared social experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(De Felice et al., 2025)</ref>, coordinated behavior and successful interpersonal communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Czeszumski et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Schilbach & Redcay, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Xie et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, meta-analytic evidence from hyperscanning studies revealed robust IBS in frontal regions and bilateral TPJ in cooperation paradigms (Czeszumski et al., 2020; Lotter et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Specifically, meta-analytic evidence from hyperscanning studies revealed robust IBS in frontal regions and bilateral TPJ in cooperation paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Czeszumski et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Lotter et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A few studies have also demonstrated that IBS in frontal regions and TPJ is associated with performance in cooperation paradigms (see e.g. Cheng et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2017; Xie et al., 2020)).
text.formatted: A few studies have also demonstrated that IBS in frontal regions and TPJ is associated with performance in cooperation paradigms (see e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cheng et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Pan et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Xie et al., 2020)</ref>).

text.text: The primary goal of relational neuroscience is to investigate how neural dynamics are associated with formation, engagement, and maintenance of social relationships, focusing on two key factors: interpersonal closeness and level of interactivity (De Felice et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The primary goal of relational neuroscience is to investigate how neural dynamics are associated with formation, engagement, and maintenance of social relationships, focusing on two key factors: interpersonal closeness and level of interactivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(De Felice et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Interpersonal closeness (i.e., degree of social proximity from strangers to romantic partners or family relationships) is a crucial and emerging topic in social neuroscience (Czeszumski et al., 2022; De Felice et al., 2025; Lotter et al., 2023; Schilbach & Redcay, 2025).
text.formatted: Interpersonal closeness (i.e., degree of social proximity from strangers to romantic partners or family relationships) is a crucial and emerging topic in social neuroscience <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Czeszumski et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">De Felice et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Lotter et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Schilbach & Redcay, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Preliminary evidence using simple coordination tasks (i.e., coordinate to press a button simultaneously) suggests that familiarity and interpersonal closeness may influence neural synchrony during social interactions.
For example, romantic partners exhibit significant IBS in the superior frontal cortex during coordination, whereas such synchrony is not observed between friends or strangers (Pan et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For example, romantic partners exhibit significant IBS in the superior frontal cortex during coordination, whereas such synchrony is not observed between friends or strangers <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Pan et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Parent-child dyads show significant IBS in the PFC during cooperation, but child-stranger dyads do not (Reindl et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Parent-child dyads show significant IBS in the PFC during cooperation, but child-stranger dyads do not <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Reindl et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, studies investigating synchrony during cooperation between siblings are missing.
Siblings are considered the longest-lasting social relationships (Cicirelli, 2013; Jensen et al., 2023) and play an important role in social, cognitive and affective development (Howe et al., 2022).

text.text: As children develop, sibling interactions provide repeated opportunities to refine their prosocial and cooperative behavior, making this behavior increasingly effective and strategic (Hughes, 2026).

text.text: Their extensive shared experiences and familiarity, combined with emotionally charged and uninhibited interactions over time, offer a unique context for understanding their own and others' minds (Paine, 2026).

text.text: Despite this, compared to other relationships, sibling relationships remain understudied (Jensen et al., 2023), accounting for only 2.5% of family systems research worldwide, compared to 65.7% on parent-child or 31.2% on couple relationships (Perez-Brena et al., 2022).

text.text: Closeness on the other hand seems to be mostly dependent on time spent together and perceived similarity (Hehman et al., 2023).

text.text: Neuroimaging evidence on sibling interactions is scarce.

Two single-brain functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies in adolescents suggest that greater similarity in mPFC during risky decision-making is associated with modeling the behavior of the other sibling (Rogers et al., 2021); and that perceived sibling closeness as measured from the perspective of the participating individual is associated with increased activation in the mPFC, anterior insula, and striatum during safe decisions in a risk-taking task (Rogers et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Two single-brain functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies in adolescents suggest that greater similarity in mPFC during risky decision-making is associated with modeling the behavior of the other sibling <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Rogers et al., 2021)</ref>; and that perceived sibling closeness as measured from the perspective of the participating individual is associated with increased activation in the mPFC, anterior insula, and striatum during safe decisions in a risk-taking task <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Rogers et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Both studies, however, are limited in their ability to capture if and how the brains of siblings interact, as adolescents performed an individual task and were scanned separately.

A single-brain analysis of a realtime interactive paradigm, showed that a competitive sibling relationship, as indicated by both siblings, predicted brain activity in frontal and precuneus regions during siblings' decisionmaking (Hernandez-Pena et al., 2024).

text.text: Little is known about brain dynamics between interacting siblings.
A relevant factor in relational neuroscience is the level of interactivity (i.e., richness of mutual exchange during social interaction) (De Felice et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A relevant factor in relational neuroscience is the level of interactivity (i.e., richness of mutual exchange during social interaction) <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(De Felice et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Studying IBS of social interaction and relationship dynamics requires ecological, real-time, dynamic and reciprocal paradigms, in which the behavior of one partner influences the other (Hakim et al., 2023; Schilbach & Redcay, 2025; Tsoi et al., 2022).

text.text: Many cooperation and coordination paradigms to date have relied on minimalistic button-pressing tasks (e.g., Baker et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2017; Sijben et al., 2025)) thereby missing emotional and relationship dynamics.

text.text: Only a few studies employed more complex, naturalistic settings with high interactivity.
These tasks could better reflect real-world interactions and place greater cognitive demands on participants (Czeszumski et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These tasks could better reflect real-world interactions and place greater cognitive demands on participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Czeszumski et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: There is a growing need for tasks involving online reciprocal interaction which unfold unpredictably and dynamically (Misaki et al., 2020).
text.formatted: There is a growing need for tasks involving online reciprocal interaction which unfold unpredictably and dynamically <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Misaki et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Such tasks require continuous realtime predictions of the interacting partners' future behavior (Schilbach & Redcay, 2025; Tsoi et al., 2022).
