text.text: Cooperative games such as "multiplayer Tetris" or "Pictionary" (Xie et al., 2020) present valuable options as they inherently involve reciprocal interaction shaped by task demands and participants' strategies.
text.formatted: Cooperative games such as "multiplayer Tetris" or "Pictionary" <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Xie et al., 2020)</ref> present valuable options as they inherently involve reciprocal interaction shaped by task demands and participants' strategies.

text.text: These games encourage participants to adapt and learn as the game progresses.
This may foster emotional engagement linked to success or failure, while capturing aspects of everyday coordination and cooperation more effectively than highly constrained paradigms.
Within the relational neuroscience framework, such tasks enable interactivity going beyond passive co-presence toward reciprocal engagement (De Felice et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Within the relational neuroscience framework, such tasks enable interactivity going beyond passive co-presence toward reciprocal engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(De Felice et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Successful social interaction depends on the continuous prediction of a partner's upcoming actions and intentions (Hamilton, 2021; Schilbach & Redcay, 2025).
text.formatted: Successful social interaction depends on the continuous prediction of a partner's upcoming actions and intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hamilton, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Schilbach & Redcay, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the Mutual Prediction Theory, IBS is thought to appear if both partners update internal models to minimize prediction error and achieve coordinated behavior (Friston & Frith, 2015).
text.formatted: In the Mutual Prediction Theory, IBS is thought to appear if both partners update internal models to minimize prediction error and achieve coordinated behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Friston & Frith, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In the novel Cooperative Tetris Task (Hernandez-Pena et al., 2023), coordinated behavior is needed to solve the task of a dropping piece that can only be placed optimally if movement and rotation of each partner are aligned.
text.formatted: In the novel Cooperative Tetris Task <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hernandez-Pena et al., 2023)</ref>, coordinated behavior is needed to solve the task of a dropping piece that can only be placed optimally if movement and rotation of each partner are aligned.

text.text: Participants need to engage in moment-to-moment monitoring and adjust to a partner's behavior that may be difficult to predict, thereby relying on continuously updating internal models.
This task thus offers a naturalistic context for testing IBS as a mechanism supporting effective coordination in siblings.
Few hyperscanning studies have studied neural synchrony during complex cooperative tasks, especially in the ToM network, and their relation to task success.

Using fMRI hyperscanning, Xie and colleagues (Xie et al., 2020) reported increased synchrony in real compared to shuffled triads during a collaborative drawing task, involving visual and somatosensory association cortices as well as dorsal attention and ToM networks; uncorrected analyses linked right posterior TPJ synchrony to team performance.
text.formatted: Using fMRI hyperscanning, Xie and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Xie et al., 2020)</ref> reported increased synchrony in real compared to shuffled triads during a collaborative drawing task, involving visual and somatosensory association cortices as well as dorsal attention and ToM networks; uncorrected analyses linked right posterior TPJ synchrony to team performance.

text.text: Another study using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning showed that synchrony in bilateral frontal regions emerged only when unacquainted triads jointly pursued a shared goal, but not during individual or observational conditions (Fishburn et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Another study using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning showed that synchrony in bilateral frontal regions emerged only when unacquainted triads jointly pursued a shared goal, but not during individual or observational conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fishburn et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, their study did not investigate the relationship between this synchrony and behavioral performance.
Similarly, greater synchrony was found in the anterior right TPJ in real versus permuted unacquainted pairs during a joint force production task (Abe et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Similarly, greater synchrony was found in the anterior right TPJ in real versus permuted unacquainted pairs during a joint force production task <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abe et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Behavioral cooperation was associated only with intrabrain activation.

Using fNIRS, prefrontal synchrony was found exclusively between real participant pairs during collaborative brainstorming (Lu & Hao, 2019), and another study reported widespread cooperation-related synchrony in real compared to permuted pairs across temporoparietal and prefrontal regions using fMRI hyperscanning (Špiláková et al., 2020).

text.text: Overall, existing hyperscanning research on complex cooperation has largely focused on unacquainted participants, relied on predefined regions of interest (ROIs), investigated small samples and rarely examined direct associations between IBS and behavioral performance.
Siblings' brain dynamics during interactions have not been studied yet.
Different levels of complexity within these cooperative tasks could help disentangle whether increased coordination demands lead to greater or reduced neural synchrony between interacting siblings.

Preliminary findings on sex differences in IBS are mixed and inconclusive, with studies using simple coordination tasks reporting higher IBS in opposite-sex pairs (Cheng et al., 2015), but also the opposite, higher coherence in same-sex pairs (right inferior PFC in male-male pairs and right temporal cortex in female-female pairs) (Baker et al., 2016), or no differences in IBS comparing same-sex pairs (Liu et al., 2023).

text.text: In the currently investigated sibling sample, we previously observed more competitive behavior and increased intra-brain activation in ToM regions in brothers compared to sisters during real-time decision-making (Hernandez-Pena et al., 2024).

text.text: Without a directional hypothesis, here we will explore IBS sex differences in sibling pairs during the Cooperative Tetris Task.

Methodologically, hyperscanning literature exhibits a topic bias (Lotter et al., 2023), with most fMRI studies focusing on game theory paradigms (M.-Y. Wang et al., 2018) and joint attention tasks (Lotter et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Methodologically, hyperscanning literature exhibits a topic bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lotter et al., 2023)</ref>, with most fMRI studies focusing on game theory paradigms (M.-Y. <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wang et al., 2018)</ref> and joint attention tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lotter et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Research on cooperation and coordination is primarily conducted using fNIRS and a few studies using electroencephalography (EEG) set-ups.

This yields three key limitations in hyperscanning cooperation research: (1) fNIRS and EEG offer lower spatial resolution than fMRI, preventing access to subcortical regions (Czeszumski et al., 2020; Misaki et al., 2020; Tsoi et al., 2022), and (2) fNIRS analyses are often restricted to a small number of predefined regions of interest (De Felice et al., 2025), particularly in frontal and temporal regions, and especially in the right hemisphere (see, for example, Liu et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2017), limiting whole-brain investigation and introducing potential biases.

text.text: Furthermore, most reviewed studies include fewer than 10 pairs (Czeszumski et al., 2020), highlighting that hyperscanning is still in its infancy (Tsoi et al., 2022), and emphasizing the need for further development of both methodology and sample size.

text.text: (3) Often hyperscanning paradigms lack complex, naturalistic settings enabling interactions that unfold unpredictably and dynamically.
In response, our study aims to expand the field of fMRI hyperscanning by employing a complex, validated cooperation task in a large sample.
By studying siblings, we additionally maximize the potential to test whether and how long-term relationship quality may interfere with behavioral coordination and neural synchrony.

Given the role of familiarity and interpersonal closeness between interaction partners for IBS during real-time cooperation, our first aim is to investigate whether real-time interacting sibling pairs show different patterns of brain synchrony compared to randomly permuted noninteracting non-sibling pairs across social brain regions.

Second, we aim to explore whether IBS is associated with sibling relationship characteristics such as mutuality (i.e., acceptance, affection, reciprocity and similarity experienced by the siblings) and competitiveness (representing the degree to which one sibling wants to outperform the other or feels envious of the other).
Furthermore, we aim to examine if the association between IBS differs depending on task performance and complexity, and sex differences between brother and sister pairs in task performance and IBS.
We pre-registered our hypotheses and analyses at the Open Science Framework prior to data collection (https://osf.io/5jbk8).
text.formatted: We pre-registered our hypotheses and analyses at the Open Science Framework prior to data collection (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/5jbk8">https://osf.io/5jbk8</ref>).

text.text: Our pre-registered hypothesis was that IBS would be higher in TPJ and PFC in interacting sibling pairs vs non-interacting non-sibling pairs.

A posteriori, we extended our synchrony analyses adding different cortical and subcortical regions from the social brain atlas (Alcalá-López et al., 2018) moving beyond analyses limited to a few predefined regions of interest to explore which social networks (processing levels: visualsensory, limbic, intermediate-level and higher-level) are more involved in real-time, cooperative interactions.
text.formatted: A posteriori, we extended our synchrony analyses adding different cortical and subcortical regions from the social brain atlas <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alcalá-López et al., 2018)</ref> moving beyond analyses limited to a few predefined regions of interest to explore which social networks (processing levels: visualsensory, limbic, intermediate-level and higher-level) are more involved in real-time, cooperative interactions.

text.text: Based on the Mutual Prediction Theory and the role of ToM processes in social cooperation, we expected higher IBS in regions from the high-level network (ToM network including bilateral TPJ, bilateral middle temporal gyri, precuneus, dorsomedial PFC, posterior cingulate cortex and medial frontal pole) than in regions from other networks (i.e., limbic, visual-sensory and intermediate processing networks) (H1).

As pre-registered, we hypothesized that a) IBS would be associated with cooperative behavior (measured as better task performance, i.e., success in the task) (H2); b) IBS would differ as a function of task complexity, with higher synchrony in easy compared to complex blocks (H3); and c) a cooperative sibling relationship would be associated with higher IBS (H4).
Additionally, we compared sex differences in performance and IBS.
Based on previous literature, we suggest better performance among brothers (male-male pairs).
Post-hoc we also investigated whether this link is mediated by higher IBS (H5).

The sample took part in a more extensive study involving a total of three tasks in the scanner, followed by a battery of selfreported questionnaires, taking approximately 3 hours to complete the whole procedure.

After voluntary written informed consent was obtained, participants received verbal instructions about the study and task instructions using pre-recorded videos to ensure consistency of instructions across pairs.
The experimenters clarified each question with systematic answers.
Participants were not allowed to communicate during the task instructions in order to prevent any prior coordination.
After debriefing at the end of the session, all participants received compensation of 60 Euros.

text.text: We defined a cooperative sibling relationship based on STQ mutuality (Cronbach's α = .909) and competition (Cronbach's α = .840) subscales, with reliability ranging from good to excellent.

The Cooperative Tetris Task (Figures 1B and 1C) is an adapted version of the classic singleplayer Tetris game, specifically designed for two players to work together to solve the predesigned puzzles collaboratively.
text.formatted: The Cooperative Tetris Task (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>) is an adapted version of the classic singleplayer Tetris game, specifically designed for two players to work together to solve the predesigned puzzles collaboratively.

text.text: For an in-depth description of the puzzles' stimuli design and task validation, please refer to Hernandez-Pena et al. (2023).

text.text: In the traditional Tetris game, players must fit falling Tetris pieces into a structure of pieces at the bottom of the playfield to complete horizontal lines.
When a line is successfully completed, it disappears, causing any remaining pieces above it to fall downwards.
In the Cooperative Tetris Task, each participant has a distinct role: one manages horizontal movement (right and left), while the other one is responsible for rotating the pieces clockwise.

Roles were randomly assigned at the beginning of the study and alternated each round (see the next paragraph for a detailed description of the task structure), ensuring that both participants fulfilled each role twice across the four total rounds.

The aim was to complete as many lines as possible; thus, participants depended on non-verbal coordination and mutual understanding to effectively position and orient the pieces to fill gaps and clear lines.
In some trials within each block, rotation or movement was not required (e.g., see Figure 1C, trial 2.2.

text.text: Pairs played four rounds of six blocks with 4 pieces (i.e., trials) each (i.e., 96 trials in total).
Each block showed a different pre-designed set of pieces already placed at the bottom of the playfield.
This way, we created a series of controlled scenarios (blocks) while allowing free interaction with the start of the first falling piece (each piece = one trial).
Each round contained three easy and three complex blocks (i.e., 24 blocks in total; 12 easy and 12 complex).

In the easy blocks, there was only one clear position to place the piece in order to clear a line, whereas in the complex scenarios, there were two equally good positions to place the piece, creating a conflict between the participants (see Figures 1B and 1C) and for further details see Hernandez-Pena et al., (2023).

text.text: If pieces were positioned as designed, participants would successfully clean four lines in the easy blocks (one per piece/trial, Figure 1B) and two lines in the complex blocks (lines were designed to be fully completed earliest in the second and fourth trials, see Figure 1C and Figure S1).

text.text: Success (cooperative performance) was measured as the number of lines completed, as pre-registered.
In total, each block lasted approximately 20s.
At the end of each block, a screen showing the result (remaining pieces) with the text "next round" served as a jittered inter-stimulus interval, which lasted between four to five seconds.
Participants completed all blocks in the same order, as preregistered.
In addition, several questions about participant experiences were collected at the end of each round (i.e., four times) (for further details see Hernandez-Pena et al., (2023).

text.text: MRI data acquisition MRI scans were performed on two Siemens 3-Tesla scanners (a Siemens MAGNETOM Prisma scanner and a MAGNETOM Prisma fit scanner, Siemens Medical Systems, Erlangen, Germany), both equipped with 20-channel head coils.
The scanners were checked for consistency in field strength, software, and gradients.

Precise synchronization between the task and the MRI scanners was achieved using a virtual server at the Brain Imaging Facility (University Hospital RWTH Aachen) using the Socket module (Python 3.6.6) over a secure TCP/IP network (Sijben et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Precise synchronization between the task and the MRI scanners was achieved using a virtual server at the Brain Imaging Facility (University Hospital RWTH Aachen) using the Socket module (Python 3.6.6) over a secure TCP/IP network <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Sijben et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Communication between the computers displaying the task at each scanner and the server was continuous, with minimal latency (maximum 16 ms).
With the latency being below the refresh rate of the screens displaying the task, this ensured that task performance was not affected.
The task was started simultaneously on both computers by signals from the server (see Figure 1A), which synchronized them at the beginning of each trial to prevent any possible desynchronization.
text.formatted: The task was started simultaneously on both computers by signals from the server (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>), which synchronized them at the beginning of each trial to prevent any possible desynchronization.

text.text: Acquisition of brain imaging data was also synchronized due to a trigger signal from the server via a parallel port to ensure that all data remained synchronized.

Structural images were acquired with a magnetization-prepared rapid acquisition gradient echo (MPRAGE) sequences with TR = 2000 ms, TE = 3.03 ms, inversion time (TI) = 90 ms, flip angle = 9°, voxel size = 1x1x1 mm, matrix size = 256x256, and number of slides = 176.

Functional images during the task were acquired using multiband echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequences with the following acquisition parameters: repetition time (TR) = 1500 ms, echo time (TE) = 34 ms, multiband acceleration factor = 3, flip angle = 70°, voxel size = 2x2x2 mm, matrix size = 96x96, and number of interleaved slides = 69.
The slices included the entire brain and were oriented transaxially parallel to the anterior-posterior commissural line and acquired in a posterior-to-anterior direction.
Task and functional scans lasted approximately between 12-17 minutes (with a total MRI scan duration of approximately one hour including all MRI sequences and other tasks).
We used fMRIPrep (Esteban et al., 2019) to preprocess our fMRI data.
text.formatted: We used fMRIPrep <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Esteban et al., 2019)</ref> to preprocess our fMRI data.

text.text: The standard preprocessing steps include discarding the first four volumes, head motion correction, skull stripping, segmentation of brain tissues, reconstruction of the brain surface, boundary-based alignment to anatomical space, and non-linear normalization to MNI space.
Next, we applied a high-pass filter of 0.01 Hz.
The frame-wise displacement (FD) metric was calculated by summing the absolute values of relative motion (Power et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The frame-wise displacement (FD) metric was calculated by summing the absolute values of relative motion <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Power et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Any volume with an FD exceeding 0.8 mm was marked as a motion outlier. fMRI data with more than 20% of volumes classified as motion outliers were excluded from further analysis.
Following the most common fMRI hyperscanning analysis strategy (Hakim et al., 2023), we here applied ISC, as pre-registered, as a measure of IBS.

text.text: This allows us to better compare our findings with other studies with different samples and designs.

To this end, we first performed a subject-level general linear model (GLM) using FSL (FMRIB, Oxford, UK) with task regressors set as events including stick functions for piece appearance, horizontal movement or rotation, successful end of the trial (indicated by a line completed), unsuccessful end of the trial (not completed line), and questions blocks.
To account for potential confounds, we partialled out 12 motion parameters, including six realignment estimates and their temporal derivatives.
Additionally, we regressed out the mean signal from white matter and cerebrospinal fluid (Fox et al., 2005), along with motion outliers identified using FD (Power et al., 2012).

text.text: We extracted time-series from the residual images, after regressing out the signals driven by the common task regressors, following the same procedure as Abe et al., (2019) and Xie et al., (2020), for 36 seeds based on the social brain atlas (Alcalá-López et al., 2018).
text.formatted: We extracted time-series from the residual images, after regressing out the signals driven by the common task regressors, following the same procedure as <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Abe et al., (2019)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Xie et al., (2020)</ref>, for 36 seeds based on the social brain atlas <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alcalá-López et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The seeds were constructed as spheres with a radius of 5 mm around the coordinates.
We averaged the extracted time-series for each seed and z-scored them.
Next, we divided the residual time-series into twelve windows of easy and complex blocks.
Pearson's correlation coefficients were calculated between residual time-series of each window and each seed within each pair of subjects.
To estimate ISC for each seed and each pair, we averaged the calculated correlation coefficients across windows within each pair of subjects per seed.

To determine seeds with ISC values above the chance level, we generated a null distribution for each seed by randomly reassigning pair labels across 10,000 iterations and calculating ISC for each permuted pair as described above.
To preserve role differences, we ensured that subjects within random pairs held the complementary role (horizontal movement vs rotation).
Finally, we determined seeds with averaged real-pair ISC values above 95% of random values after correcting for multiple comparisons using false discovery rate (FDR; Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

Brain-behavior relationships Regression models were implemented to examine the relationship between ISC values and behavioral measures.
First, we regressed task performance against ISC values to investigate how neural synchronization influenced performance within interacting pairs.
The performance was defined as the total number of lines cleaned by each pair during the task (Hernandez-Pena et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The performance was defined as the total number of lines cleaned by each pair during the task <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hernandez-Pena et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Next, to assess whether synchronization is associated with task complexity, we compared ISC values across the two conditions (easy vs complex blocks) using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
As a validation, to ensure differences between easy and complex blocks, we compared task performance across blocks using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
Here, we adjusted performance scores by multiplying scores in complex blocks by two to make them comparable between the two conditions.

To investigate whether a mutual cooperative and a competitive sibling relationship are associated with ISC, we regressed ISC values for each seed against averaged pair scores from the STQ mutuality and competition subscales.

To test the differences between siblings' scores in relation to IBS, we implemented supplementary models using the same subscales but based on the absolute differences in sibling scores instead of averages.

As we only assumed that synchrony measures were valid if the seed showed significantly higher ISC in real-time compared to permuted pairs, regression models were fitted separately only for each of these validated seeds.
The results were corrected for multiple comparisons using FDR correction.
Lastly, we implemented an independent t-test to examine task performance differences across female-female and male-male sibling pairs.
To test whether the relationship between sex and performance was mediated by ISC, we conducted a mediation analysis per seed.
The analyses were performed using the mediation package (Tingley et al., 2014) in RStudio (version 4.3.1) using a bootstrapping approach with 1000 simulations.

In this study, we observed significant synchrony in interacting sibling pairs, compared to randomly permuted non-interacting non-sibling dyads performing the same cooperative task, across cortical and subcortical regions defined in the social brain atlas (Alcalá-López et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In this study, we observed significant synchrony in interacting sibling pairs, compared to randomly permuted non-interacting non-sibling dyads performing the same cooperative task, across cortical and subcortical regions defined in the social brain atlas <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alcalá-López et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We particularly found synchrony between siblings in the high-level subnetwork (associated with mentalizing abilities) and intermediate-level subnetwork (associated with sensory and motor processing, and empathy).
Moreover, higher synchrony in the left TPJ of interacting siblings was associated with greater cooperative success.

Our findings are in line with previous studies in unacquainted participants finding higher brain synchrony in frontal and temporal regions for interacting vs. randomly permuted pairs/triads employing cooperative tasks (e.g., Pictionary, puzzles) (Abe et al., 2019; Fishburn et al., 2018; Špiláková et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Our findings are in line with previous studies in unacquainted participants finding higher brain synchrony in frontal and temporal regions for interacting vs. randomly permuted pairs/triads employing cooperative tasks (e.g., Pictionary, puzzles) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abe et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Fishburn et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Špiláková et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Xie et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Using the social brain atlas (Alcalá-López et al., 2018), we could further investigate whether different social networks are equally involved during social interactions.
text.formatted: Using the social brain atlas <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alcalá-López et al., 2018)</ref>, we could further investigate whether different social networks are equally involved during social interactions.

text.text: Interestingly, we observed that higher synchrony, comparing interacting sibling vs. randomly permuted pairs, was predominantly observed in the high-level and intermediate-level subnetworks.
The visual-sensory and limbic subnetworks showed only a few synchronized seeds during cooperative interactions.

This pattern is consistent with the functional specialization of these networks as described by the original meta-analysis authors (Alcalá-López et al., 2018): the high-level subnetworks support the inference of others' mental states, and the intermediate-level subnetworks are involved in empathy, salience, and the integration of sensory input with motor planning.
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with the functional specialization of these networks as described by the original meta-analysis authors <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alcalá-López et al., 2018)</ref>: the high-level subnetworks support the inference of others' mental states, and the intermediate-level subnetworks are involved in empathy, salience, and the integration of sensory input with motor planning.

text.text: The visual-sensory and limbic subnetworks respond to facial and biologically relevant cues associated with perception-action.

In our task, these subnetworks may have been less engaged because participants could neither see nor hear each other, reducing the relevance of such cues, compared to other hyperscanning set-ups in a face-to-face situation.
In the absence of visual cues, mentalizing abilities are particularly relevant for inferring others' intentions and predicting their future actions.

The ToM network is especially important for processing social interactions (Lotter et al., 2023; Votinov et al., 2021) and specifically cooperation (Czeszumski et al., 2020; Sijben et al., 2025; L.-S. Wang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The ToM network is especially important for processing social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lotter et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Votinov et al., 2021)</ref> and specifically cooperation <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Czeszumski et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Sijben et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">L.-S. Wang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The increased synchrony in interacting pairs compared to random pairs in ToM regions strongly suggests that an alignment in micro-actions during cooperative tasks takes place without verbal communication or visual contact.
This seems to be supported by increased synchrony in motor processing regions, most likely to coordinate the actions.

Our findings align with the Mutual Prediction Theory (Hamilton, 2021), whereby IBS appears as siblings continuously update internal models to minimize prediction errors trying to predict their own and their partners' actions to coordinate the Tetris actions.
text.formatted: Our findings align with the Mutual Prediction Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hamilton, 2021)</ref>, whereby IBS appears as siblings continuously update internal models to minimize prediction errors trying to predict their own and their partners' actions to coordinate the Tetris actions.

text.text: In the Cooperation Tetris Task, ISC likely reflects the convergence of neural systems that encode self-generated behavior (e.g., anterior insula), those that forecast the partner's behavior (e.g., TPJ and mPFC), and those that encode dynamic interpersonal alignment (e.g., IFG) (Kingsbury & Hong, 2020; Lotter et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In the Cooperation Tetris Task, ISC likely reflects the convergence of neural systems that encode self-generated behavior (e.g., anterior insula), those that forecast the partner's behavior (e.g., TPJ and mPFC), and those that encode dynamic interpersonal alignment (e.g., IFG) <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kingsbury & Hong, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Lotter et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Higher synchrony within ToM regions might suggest that siblings were actively modelling each other's intentions and updating their behavior in real time.
The Cooperative Tetris task inherently requires this dynamic mutual prediction, offering an ecological means to observe these processes as they unfold.

Similar to other cooperative tasks, this task requires a high degree of mutual prediction (Hamilton, 2021), meaning that participants must predict each other's actions to achieve the same objective (target position).
text.formatted: Similar to other cooperative tasks, this task requires a high degree of mutual prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hamilton, 2021)</ref>, meaning that participants must predict each other's actions to achieve the same objective (target position).

text.text: In line with the Mutual Prediction Theory, similar patterns of TPJ activation were observed in the pairs that were better in deciding for the same position and thus -if coordination worked-were more successful in the cooperative task.

In general, a correlated BOLD signal can be understood as the similarity of signal amplitudes during transient brain activation of a common shared cognitive process; i.e. people show similar cognitive or emotional responses, for example an alignment in their ToM systems (Misaki et al., 2020), as well as how two variables, in this case neural data from homologous brain regions, co-vary over time (Hakim et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In general, a correlated BOLD signal can be understood as the similarity of signal amplitudes during transient brain activation of a common shared cognitive process; i.e. people show similar cognitive or emotional responses, for example an alignment in their ToM systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Misaki et al., 2020)</ref>, as well as how two variables, in this case neural data from homologous brain regions, co-vary over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hakim et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: To distinguish inter-brain synchrony from the interbrain relation linked to identical stimuli and task demands presented to both participants, permutation analysis is the gold standard procedure (real vs. randomly selected pairs) uncovering the genuine interaction between partners within the pair (Czeszumski et al., 2020), beyond shared sensory input (De Felice et al., 2025).

text.text: To assess pair-specific state-related brain activation, distinct from task-evoked activation, residual time series inter-brain analyses are necessary (Hakim et al., 2023).

text.text: We observed a robust positive association of synchrony in left TPJ and performance in the Tetris task.
We also found weak associations between performance and synchrony in right V5 area, left supramarginal gyrus, right IFG and anterior middle cingulate cortex (significant at an uncorrected level).
TPJ and IFG are proposed to be central hubs of the mutual social attention system, allowing for "coupling" between interacting partner (Gvirts & Perlmutter, 2020).
text.formatted: TPJ and IFG are proposed to be central hubs of the mutual social attention system, allowing for "coupling" between interacting partner <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gvirts & Perlmutter, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, it was the left TPJ rather than the right TPJ that was associated with success, which is not in line with several findings in the hyperscanning research domain (Tang et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Interestingly, it was the left TPJ rather than the right TPJ that was associated with success, which is not in line with several findings in the hyperscanning research domain <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Tang et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Zhou et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Even during collaboration, synchrony in the right TPJ has been found to be associated with success (Xie et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Even during collaboration, synchrony in the right TPJ has been found to be associated with success <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Xie et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, most studies did not explicitly exclude the possibility that synchrony in the left TPJ could also contribute, as this region was not tested.

Part of the lack of consistent results may be explained as a potential publication bias in the hyperscanning literature with researchers concentrating on the right TPJ and choosing it as a region of interest (Lotter et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Part of the lack of consistent results may be explained as a potential publication bias in the hyperscanning literature with researchers concentrating on the right TPJ and choosing it as a region of interest <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lotter et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, the nature of the task may be decisive and may document the visual and perspectivetaking requirements in the Cooperative Tetris Task.
Indeed, previous studies may imply differences with respect to a lateralization of the TPJ.

In a strategic game theory task (Ogawa & Kameda, 2019), the left TPJ was activated during the choice phase (i.e., thinking about what the other player might do and adjusting one's own behavior accordingly), while the right TPJ was involved in the feedback phase (processing of the outcome when both decisions are shown).
text.formatted: In a strategic game theory task <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Ogawa & Kameda, 2019)</ref>, the left TPJ was activated during the choice phase (i.e., thinking about what the other player might do and adjusting one's own behavior accordingly), while the right TPJ was involved in the feedback phase (processing of the outcome when both decisions are shown).

text.text: The authors concluded that the left TPJ is involved in strategic decision-making, enabling active learning from the other player's prior actions and inferring their future actions.
In contrast, the right TPJ was associated with the perception of human agency.

Meta-analytic evidence also suggests that the left TPJ plays a crucial role in visual perspective-taking (i.e., the ability to distinguish another person's visual perspective) and ToM abilities (false belief task) (Schurz et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic evidence also suggests that the left TPJ plays a crucial role in visual perspective-taking (i.e., the ability to distinguish another person's visual perspective) and ToM abilities (false belief task) <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Schurz et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Using forward inference, a meta-analysis reported the left TPJ to be more functionally specialized in action imagination compared to the right TPJ, while the right TPJ has a stronger role in social cognition, in terms of encoding, retrieving and storing information (Alcalá-López et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Using forward inference, a meta-analysis reported the left TPJ to be more functionally specialized in action imagination compared to the right TPJ, while the right TPJ has a stronger role in social cognition, in terms of encoding, retrieving and storing information <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alcalá-López et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In our Cooperative Tetris Task, the latter may not be specifically relevant as Tetris is an imagery-competing task (Agren et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In our Cooperative Tetris Task, the latter may not be specifically relevant as Tetris is an imagery-competing task <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Agren et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, participants did not see or talk to each other, thus focusing on the visual pattern of the other player was the main possibility to understand the other and to interact.

Therefore, in our task, the visual component and thereby taking the perspective of the other was more relevant than in other tasks that require mentalizing skills with a greater focus on emotions or beliefs or tasks involving face-to-face interaction.
In summary, left TPJ synchrony in the Cooperation Tetris Task likely reflects shared perspective-taking and action planning rather than abstract mental state reasoning and face-to-face interaction.

An alternative interpretation might be that pairs with better performance have a more similar representation of the scenarios thus planning their actions more similarly independent of the other's actions.
Contrary to our preregistered hypothesis, ISC did not differ between easy and complex task blocks.
One possible explanation is that ToM and other social cognition processes were necessary for both conditions.
It is possible that during easy blocks, participants were similarly thinking about their partner's intentions and actions.
The overall cognitive demands of realtime coordination, role complementarity and time pressure may have overshadowed differences in specific decision ambiguity.
In addition, the operationalization of complex blocks in the Cooperative Tetris Task may not have been strong enough at the neural level to induce differential synchrony.

Although complex blocks included trials with two equally viable target positions creating a conflict, each complex block also contained two easy trials, potentially diluting condition-specific effects when synchrony was averaged across blocks.
Future studies could investigate other dynamic measures that are not captured by ISC, such as leader-follower dynamics, which could differ with complexity.
Contrary to our hypothesis, we did not find robust evidence for associations between sibling relationship characteristics and ISC.
We did not test sibling interactions against strangers, which is why we cannot conclude that the sibling relationship itself may have a significant influence.
Furthermore, heterogeneity of the relationship quality was rather low in our sample.

Yet, one interpretation is that long-term relationship quality may, in contrast to our expectations, not facilitate mutual prediction during real-time cooperation; siblings who perceive their relationship as more mutual or less competitive do not seem to be better at predicting each other's actions in a real-time cooperation task.

While interpersonal closeness may modulate IBS (De Felice et al., 2025), its effects depend on the sample (i.e., parent-child, friends, strangers), sufficient variance across the interpersonal closeness dimension, and may interact with the specific interactivity context.
text.formatted: While interpersonal closeness may modulate IBS <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(De Felice et al., 2025)</ref>, its effects depend on the sample (i.e., parent-child, friends, strangers), sufficient variance across the interpersonal closeness dimension, and may interact with the specific interactivity context.

text.text: Moreover, mutuality in relationships does not equal closeness and may not reflect the current state in the relationship but a more general evaluation of the relationship.

Although no robust association provided support for our hypothesis, we still observed weak associations between sibling relationship characteristics (i.e., how siblings perceived their relationship) and IBS, with several regions showing weak effects that were significant at an uncorrected level.

Higher levels of mutuality between siblings (i.e., similarity, reciprocity and affection) were associated with increased ISC in the anterior insula which is associated with salience processing and social cognition (Menon & Uddin, 2010), and decreased ISC in the supramarginal gyrus, linked to self-other distinction (Quesque & Brass, 2019).
text.formatted: Higher levels of mutuality between siblings (i.e., similarity, reciprocity and affection) were associated with increased ISC in the anterior insula which is associated with salience processing and social cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Menon & Uddin, 2010)</ref>, and decreased ISC in the supramarginal gyrus, linked to self-other distinction <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Quesque & Brass, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We cautiously suggest that larger and more heterogeneous samples will reveal if these associations are robust indicators.

Considering our results as hypothesis-generating, we speculate that more supportive sibling relationships might facilitate shared engagement while reducing the need for explicit self-other differentiation during cooperation.

Similarly, greater competitiveness (i.e., reflecting efforts to outperform the other) was associated with reduced ISC in frontal pole, a region related to goal-directed action (Hogeveen et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Similarly, greater competitiveness (i.e., reflecting efforts to outperform the other) was associated with reduced ISC in frontal pole, a region related to goal-directed action <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hogeveen et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Synchrony in this region may indicate an outcome-focused strategy in only one of the siblings or different outcome evaluation; yet this also needs to be further substantiated in future studies.
Especially considering the weak statistical robustness and the reverse inference, these findings and their interpretation require replication.
Weak associations between lower ISC and divergences in the perceived sibling relationship further substantiate that relational similarity may contribute to neural alignment.

For example, greater disagreement between siblings in perceived competitiveness was associated with lower synchrony in the left TPJ (significant at an uncorrected level), suggesting that discrepancies in how competitive the relationship is perceived by each sibling may hinder shared neural processing during cooperation.
Based on this preliminary evidence, we recommend future research to explore further the role of frontal and temporal regions in the association between synchrony and familiarity.
There may be further explanations that limit our conclusions.
First, our sample was quite homogeneous and the variability in the sibling questionnaires was low.
Additionally, siblings' relationships were evaluated overall as good, probably as part of a recruitment strategy relying on siblings joining the study together.

These results might differ in a clinical or high-risk sample, which warrants further investigation -particularly in relation to mental health biomarkers associated with social deficits (De Felice et al., 2025; Lotter et al., 2023).
text.formatted: These results might differ in a clinical or high-risk sample, which warrants further investigation -particularly in relation to mental health biomarkers associated with social deficits <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(De Felice et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Lotter et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the applied questionnaires capture general relationships but not day-to-day experiences, which might be more related to our collaboration task.
Future studies could collect day-to-day cooperation data, as well as measure how much time the siblings spend together in real life using ecological momentary assessment.
Future research should move beyond ISC as the main brain dynamic measure and consider asymmetrical and complementary brain coupling in interactive dynamics.
In cooperative tasks with distinct roles, effective coordination may rely on temporally lagged or functionally complementary neural processes rather than mirrored activity (Misaki et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In cooperative tasks with distinct roles, effective coordination may rely on temporally lagged or functionally complementary neural processes rather than mirrored activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Misaki et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, effective coordination may involve asymmetric or leader-follower dynamics, wherein brain activity is temporally lagged or functionally distinct rather than aligned.
Furthermore, research should clarify how other aspects of familiarity, age difference, and role assignment might shape ISC between siblings.
Since ISC is non-directional, the direction of influence remains unclear.
Granger causality or dynamic causal modelling (Bilek et al., 2022) might be effective strategies for determining direction of influence and further investigating leader-follower dynamics.
text.formatted: Granger causality or dynamic causal modelling <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bilek et al., 2022)</ref> might be effective strategies for determining direction of influence and further investigating leader-follower dynamics.

text.text: Additionally, ROI-by-ROI analyses are statistically costly and conceptually limited; therefore, using graph theory approaches might be relevant (Lotter et al., 2023; Tsoi et al., 2022), especially in association with relationship (e.g., high mutuality may relate to greater network efficiency).
text.formatted: Additionally, ROI-by-ROI analyses are statistically costly and conceptually limited; therefore, using graph theory approaches might be relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lotter et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Tsoi et al., 2022)</ref>, especially in association with relationship (e.g., high mutuality may relate to greater network efficiency).

text.text: We further recommend applying day-to-day measures to capture the various facets of sibling relationships beyond stable characteristics and consider clinical samples as especially interesting in terms of interpersonal dynamics.
Our findings should be considered in light of several limitations.
We did not investigate intrabrain activity because it was outside the scope of this manuscript.

Although we observed significant synchrony between interacting siblings compared to randomly permuted non-sibling pairs, to claim whether there is something unique about siblings, we would need to include other control groups (such as unacquainted pairs, or familiar pairs such as parent-child, couple or friends).
We restricted our sample to same-sex sibling pairs due to the time and funding limitations of the current study.

The main reasons for not including a control group of nonsibling pairs were (a) sample size, as we would have needed to duplicate our sample size and (b) the challenge to control for factors such as long-term co-residence or shared genetics that might influence brain and behavior dynamics (Hernandez-Pena et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The main reasons for not including a control group of nonsibling pairs were (a) sample size, as we would have needed to duplicate our sample size and (b) the challenge to control for factors such as long-term co-residence or shared genetics that might influence brain and behavior dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hernandez-Pena et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should aim to replicate these results and investigate whether siblings exhibit distinctive patterns of cooperation and competition compared to non-related pairs.
Also, our study did not include an active control condition, i.e. participants playing the same task without interaction, due to time restrictions.
Accordingly, we cannot exclude the possibility that the observed ISC was driven by the remaining task components rather than the interaction itself.
However, we adopted a common approach for removing activation patterns driven by shared task structure as done in previous hyperscanning literature (Abe et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2020).
text.formatted: However, we adopted a common approach for removing activation patterns driven by shared task structure as done in previous hyperscanning literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abe et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Xie et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Notwithstanding these limitations, the present study offers several important strengths.
To our knowledge, this study represents one of the largest fMRI hyperscanning studies to date (M.-Y. Wang et al., 2018).
text.formatted: To our knowledge, this study represents one of the largest fMRI hyperscanning studies to date (M.-Y. <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Wang et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, this is the first study to investigate synchrony between sibling pairs.

Crucially, the neural dynamics of sibling cooperation cannot be captured by scanning either partner in isolation; they are an emergent property of the interaction itself, making hyperscanning not just a methodological choice but a theoretical necessity for studying this question.

Moreover, the use of a novel, ecologically valid, role-complementary cooperative task allows for continuous, reciprocal interaction that more closely resembles real-world coordination than traditional turn-based or simple coordination tasks that dominate the hyperscanning literature.
Finally, the use of the social brain atlas moves beyond narrowly defined regions of interest, providing a more comprehensive characterization of brain synchrony across social cognition systems.

In this preregistered fMRI hyperscanning study of 50 same-sex sibling pairs, we observed that inter-brain synchrony during real-time cooperation was significantly higher in interacting siblings than in randomly permuted non-siblings.

This synchrony was most prominent within high-level mentalizing and intermediate social processing networks, including bilateral TPJ, precuneus and prefrontal regions, suggesting that cooperation relies on shared predictive models of a partner's intentions and actions.
Notably, synchrony in the left TPJ predicted cooperative success, underscoring the importance of shared perspective-taking and action planning in complementary interactions.

Overall, this study advances second-person approaches and relational neuroscience by extending hyperscanning research to young adult sibling pairs -long-term familiar and understudied dyads -engaged in complex, complementary cooperative interaction.

This work complements existing studies of unacquainted pairs and other familiar dyads and opens new avenues for understanding how interpersonal closeness and sibling relationship may influence neural dynamics of real-time social interaction.

text.text: B. BOLD signals for each seed were divided into 24 blocks of easy and complex conditions.

ISC was then defined as the average of correlation coefficients across all blocks per seed.

The red line shows the average ISC across all real pairs.
